correctness.rationale: Writing \(w_i=P_i^n-P_{i-1}^n\) and \(s_i=w_i/p_i\) gives \(\mathbb E M_n-\mathbb E X=\langle X-\mathbb EX,S-1\rangle_p\), with strictly increasing score coordinates. Cauchy--Schwarz gives the stated upper endpoint and equality exactly for an increasing affine function of S. For the lower bound, every centered increasing support has the positive gap decomposition \(y=\sum_j d_jv^{(j)}\). Each threshold vector has ratio \((P_j-P_j^n)/\sqrt{P_j(1-P_j)}\), so positivity plus the triangle inequality yields the lower bound. With \(m\ge3\), at least two positive gaps multiply noncollinear threshold vectors, making the norm triangle inequality strict. Concentrating all but one gap to zero approaches the minimizing threshold ray. After quotienting translation and positive scale, positive gap vectors form a connected open simplex; continuity therefore makes the image the full interval from the unattained infimum to the attained maximum. An independent random-profile calculation over 200 profiles/supports reproduced \(L<R\le U\).

value.rationale: The upper expected-maximum geometry for discrete distributions is an established optimization problem. Determining the opposite sharp endpoint when the atom masses are fixed, including all near-minimizing shapes and every attainable intermediate value, gives the complementary geometry of the same natural statistic. The equal-mass formula and two-point boundary make the result directly reusable.
residual_risks: The practical importance depends on treating the mass profile as fixed rather than estimated or variable.

final_claim: For fixed positive masses \(\mathbf p=(p_1,\ldots,p_m)\) on strictly increasing support points and fixed sample size \(n\ge2\), the standardized expected-maximum gap has exact range \((L_n(\mathbf p),U_n(\mathbf p)]\) when \(m\ge3\), with \(L_n\) the minimum cut ratio \((P_j-P_j^n)/\sqrt{P_j(1-P_j)}\) and \(U_n\) the projection norm \(\sqrt{\sum_i w_i^2/p_i-1}\); the upper endpoint is attained exactly by an affine score support, the lower endpoint is approached by a two-level collapse, and for \(m=2\) both endpoints coincide.
limitations: Finite discrete iid parents with a fixed strictly positive atom-probability profile.
The lower endpoint is generally an infimum rather than an attained minimum because atoms must remain distinct.
